issues.issue: The parenthetical defined terms are mangled: "CSi Agency Services, Ino. (“CS”)" defines the short name "CS" while every operative section uses "CSi," and "Alpha Partners, Ltd, Alpha”)" opens no quotation mark. The mechanical error leaves the identity of the defined parties to be construed against sections III and X, which impose or release obligations by short name.

The recital defines "the reinsurance relationship" to include "all addenda to each those agreements, including, but not limited to," three named addenda, so the enumerated specifics do not bound the catch-all. Which further addenda are swept into the defined relationship, and thus into the LPT obligation in section I, is left open.

The obligation is to "enter into a Loss Portfolio Transfer Reinsurance Agreement" whose terms, premium, conditions and form are nowhere stated, so the provision is an agreement to make a future agreement. A court must decide whether "shall enter into" is an enforceable promise or leaves essential terms open.

Section IX describes the same document as "a mutually agreeable reinsurance agreement/LPT" and provides a remedy for the parties being "not able to complete" it, which cannot be squared with section I's unconditional "shall enter into" by June 30, 2009. Whether failure to execute the LPT is a breach of section I or merely triggers section IX must be construed.

The carve-out for "payments completed prior to May 4, 2009" is measured by a definition (section I's "completed" sentence) keyed solely to checks "dated and issued by Santa Fe," leaving pre-May 4 payments made by Lincoln General or out of the ZBA unaddressed. The two sentences read together do not say who bears those payments.

"Completed" is defined by the conjunctive test "dated and issued by Santa Fe," which gives no answer when a check is dated before May 4, 2009 but issued after (or the reverse). The provision also fixes the test only for checks issued by Santa Fe, not by any other party.

Permission to use the ZBA ends "until the LPT is executed, but no later than June 30, 2009," yet section IX expressly contemplates that the LPT may never be executed, leaving no mechanism for funding claims after June 30, 2009. The two provisions cannot both be given effect without construing which controls.

"[T]he date of execution" is unspecified — execution of the LPT or execution of this Memorandum of Understanding — and the same phrase reappears in the following reimbursement sentence. The cut-off for ZBA checks therefore has two readings on the face of the sentence.

The reimbursement duty is stated with no time for performance and no interest, so when Santa Fe must repay ZBA draws is left at large. "[T]he date of execution" likewise takes its meaning only from the preceding sentence.

The $3 million is said to be "partial security" and expressly "not ... a limitation on those obligations," but the final sentence of the same section caps posted security at "not exceed $3 million." Whether Santa Fe can ever be required to post more than $3 million must be construed between the two.

Option (b) requires "an A rated reinsurer" without naming the rating agency or the date the rating is measured, and option (a) requires "other investments acceptable to Lincoln General" with no standard of acceptability. Both terms leave the sufficiency of the security to one party's undefined judgment.

The requirement that Lincoln General "be permitted to participate in the drafting and wording of the agreement" sets no measure of participation or of what terms the reinsurance agreement must contain. Whether a reinsurance placement satisfies section II therefore turns on an unstated standard.

This sentence caps the collateral at "not exceed $3 million" for "the amount of future losses forecast," which conflicts with the opening of section II stating the $3 million is "partial security" and "not ... a limitation on those obligations." A court must decide whether the cap limits Santa Fe's security duty after a reinsurer default.

Release of trust funds whenever market value merely "is greater than" Santa Fe's estimated remaining liability cannot be squared with section II(a), under which the escrowed funds "shall only be able to be withdrawn with Lincoln General's consent" and secure the whole $3 million. Whether the entire corpus, or only the excess, may be released is unstated.

"This release shall be performed annually" is mandatory, while the preceding sentence says the funds "may be released" — permissive — only if a market-value test is met. The two sentences of section II cannot both be given effect without construing whether the annual release is compulsory, and from what date the year runs.

Santa Fe's duty to fund "all activities" for claims under the 2002 and 2003 agreements carries no start date, whereas section I excludes from Santa Fe's liability any payment "completed prior to May 4, 2009." Whether section III reaches pre-May 4, 2009 claim activity must be construed against that exclusion.

The catch-all "any other expenses related to claims investigation, settlement, contesting, and handling" sits against an enumerated list of claim payments, attorney's fees and legal expenses, leaving its outer bound unfixed. Whether it reaches, for example, Lincoln General's own litigation or administrative costs is open.

The preservation of "any obligations of U.S. Auto, Gamma, or any other defendant" cannot be squared with section X, under which the contemplated settlement agreement will "provide for releases of all Defendants" upon Santa Fe's performance. Which provision governs the other defendants' continuing liability must be construed.

The installment schedule begins January 2, 2010 and runs to 2014 regardless of whether the LPT and settlement agreement are ever executed, while section IX provides that if those documents are not completed Lincoln General's remedy "shall be to refile the lawsuit." Whether the note payments survive a section IX failure is unaddressed.

The note must be "in a form substantially similar to Exhibit A," but no Exhibit A is attached to the executed Memorandum of Understanding. The referenced form is missing from the instrument, and "substantially similar" supplies no standard in its absence.

The parties' stipulation that the Memorandum is "sufficiently definite to allow the parties to sue for its enforcement" cannot be squared with section IX, which limits Lincoln General's remedy for non-completion to refiling the lawsuit. Whether suit on the Memorandum or refiling the dismissed case is available must be construed between the two.

"[S]ufficiently definite to allow the parties to sue for its enforcement" is a recitation of a legal conclusion, and the provision does not say which obligations it is definite as to. Whether the parties can contract themselves out of indefiniteness as to sections I and X is left to construction.

"[T]olling and other litigation resumption agreements" names no form, no terms and no deadline, and "other litigation resumption agreements" has no defined content beyond the tolling example. It is an undertaking to execute unspecified future documents.

The tolling runs "for five (5) years of until all claims ... have been paid and settled," where the mangled conjunction leaves it unclear whether the period is five years, or until all claims are paid, or the longer or shorter of the two. "[P]aid and settled ... pursuant to any and all agreements between them" also fixes no ascertainable end date.

The provision incorporates the "Other Causes of Action" defined in "the April 28, 2008 letter agreement," but the letter agreement in the record is dated April 30, 2008. The misdescription puts in issue which document, and hence which definition, is being incorporated.

The April 2008 letter tolls the Other Causes of Action "until the Lawsuit has been settled or otherwise finally resolved, including the completion of any appeals," while section VI tolls them for five years or until all claims are paid. Which tolling term governs those causes of action after the Lawsuit's dismissal cannot be answered from either document alone.

Tolling is extended only to defenses, counterclaims and equitable theories the Defendants "are asserting in the Lawsuit at the time of its dismissal," which by its terms excludes theories not yet pleaded when the case was dismissed. What it means to "toll" a defense, as opposed to a claim, is also left unstated.

"[T]he same limitations posture as they had in the lawsuit prior to its dismissal" is an undefined phrase that does not say whether accrual, filing date, or relation-back is what is preserved. It must be read against the five-year toll in the same section to know which controls.

"[S]ubject to regulatory approval" identifies no regulator, no applicant, no deadline, and no consequence if approval is refused or never sought. Whether it is a condition precedent to the whole Memorandum or only to the LPT is unresolved on its face.

Making the Memorandum "and the matters to which it addresses" subject to regulatory approval cannot be squared with section V, under which the Memorandum is enforceable on execution and Lincoln General must immediately dismiss its case. Which provision fixes the moment of binding effect must be construed.

The heading covers "Failure to Complete the Required Actions ... or Later Breach," but the operative text addresses only the parties being "not able to complete" the contemplated documents and says nothing about breach. Whether refiling is also the remedy for a later breach, and whether it is an exclusive remedy at all, is left open.

Limiting Lincoln General's remedy to refiling the lawsuit cannot be squared with section V's agreement that the Memorandum is "sufficiently definite to allow the parties to sue for its enforcement," nor with the unconditional payment duty in section IV. A court must decide whether section IX displaces enforcement of the Memorandum.

The parties merely "agree to draft a settlement agreement" that will, "among other things," provide releases, leaving the releases' scope, parties, timing and remaining terms entirely for future negotiation. It is on its face an agreement to agree.

"[T]he particulars of the releases in Defendants' favor" and "that agreement's other terms" are wholly deferred to a document not yet drafted, so nothing in this provision fixes who is released or from what. The provision states an intention without any ascertainable content.

"[S]uch other and further documents and/or pleadings as may be reasonably necessary" sets no standard for what is reasonably necessary and no time for performance. Read with sections I and X it could be argued to compel execution of the LPT and settlement agreement whose terms are undetermined.
